extracted.intended_audience: aspiring reporters, journalism students, and newspaper staff (reporters, editors, press and business managers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing newspaper content and operating a newspaper (news judgment, writing, sourcing, printing, and business/ circulation/advertising roles). Intended to train reporters and newspaper managers in daily practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of News Writing (four requisites)
rubrics_metrics.description: To write successful news stories, four requisites are necessary: the power to estimate news values properly, the stories to write, the ability to work rapidly, and the power to present facts accurately and interestingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each requisite is essential: recognize what is newsworthy, have a substantive story to file, work with speed under deadline, and present facts both accurately and in an engaging manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nose for News
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of news values — the intuitive ability to recognize a story when one sees it — is essential for a reporter's success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many would-be reporters fail because they cannot recognize news; training and analysis of news qualities are necessary. Example anti-pattern: a correspondent who reports only trivial local happenings and misses serious stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of News
rubrics_metrics.description: News is any accurate fact or idea that will interest a large number of readers; of two stories the accurate one that interests the greater number of people is the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features such as strangeness, abnormality, unexpectedness, and nearness add interest but are not essential. Timeliness is useful but not required (e.g., discovery of an old but important fact can still be news).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (Accuracy First)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy is paramount: if a piece of news is untrue it is worthless and undermines public confidence; first-class papers aim never to be forced to retract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rumors may be published only as unverified rumor. Emphasize verification; avoid publishing unverified facts as established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest (provokes thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: A news item must present a new problem or situation that will provoke thought in a considerable number of readers; the most interesting stories present new problems to the greatest number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest is psychological: readers engage with new problems. Stories that merely repeat familiar situations without a new angle are less valuable. Examples: crime, divorce, or unusual events because they introduce fresh problems or phases of problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness greatly adds to a story's interest — using immediacy markers like 'to-day', 'this morning', 'this afternoon' makes pieces more valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close competition and improved machinery have made freshness often requisite; however, timeliness is not strictly essential to be newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closeness of Event (nearness in time/place)
rubrics_metrics.description: The worth of a story generally varies inversely with distance in time and place; nearer events (geographically or temporally) have greater value to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should localize stories when possible (local angles, local persons' opinions) to increase relevance. A small local theft may outrank a larger distant theft for local readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for Extremes (record-breaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are the largest, smallest, fastest, foulest, boldest, etc., attract interest as record-breaking or extreme occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should seek extremes because they present new problems or notable departures from the norm and thus command attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Unusual (exceptional/abnormal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exceptional, unusual, or abnormal occurrences (e.g., a two-headed calf, odd moral reversals) are inherently interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unusual incidents are classed with record-breaking items and should be highlighted for their novelty and reader appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contests (struggle for supremacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of contests — athletic, business, political, or social struggles — make interesting news because the element of struggle is universally appealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injecting conflict or competition into a story adds zest; look for contests in many arenas (politics, labor, business, sports, society).

rubrics_metrics.name: Helplessness (emotional appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories portraying the joys or sufferings of the very old, very young, or those unable to struggle emotionally compel reader sympathy and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Sob stories’ that show friendlessness or want can be both widely read and practically helpful; reporters often seek such human-interest pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominent Persons
rubrics_metrics.description: News about prominent men and women attracts interest proportionate to their prominence; trivial acts by the famous are still newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers care about figures of high social or professional position even if they do not personally know them; highlight prominence as a hook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-known Places
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories associated with noted or notorious places (e.g., Reno, Coney Island, Niagara Falls) have enhanced interest by virtue of prior note or notoriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, fix the setting in a well-known place to increase reader engagement and reprintability across regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal and Financial Interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that directly affect the personal or financial interests of readers (prices, taxes, supplies, fashions) are especially likely to be read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should monitor markets, shops, and trade to spot items affecting readers' pocketbooks or household concerns; such items can often be obtained by casual visits to merchants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Prerequisite: Accuracy + New Situation
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental prerequisites for story material are that it be accurate and possess interest by presenting a new situation or a new phase of an old situation/problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While many features (timeliness, locality, prominence) add value, none supersede the requirement of truth and the presence of a new or newly-framed problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: News Sources: beats and runs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular sources (beats or runs) — offices, departments, and institutions — are the principal supply of news (e.g., police, coroner, county clerk, health department, hotels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reporter should cultivate and regularly visit assigned beats to gather predictable flows of news; beats generate slips, arrest sheets, licenses, permits, and other paper trails useful for quick, accurate stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police Slips and Arrest Sheets as primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Police 'slips' (bulletins) and 'arrest sheets' provide brief but prompt and accurate accounts of accidents, crimes, and arrests; they are open to public inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters use these for quick follow-up; slips show time, officer, precinct details. Not all police reports are public; some information is withheld to avoid jeopardizing arrests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular News Sources (detailed beats list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific beats and the kinds of news found there: Associated Charities (relief/destitution), Boards of Trade (market quotations), Boxing Commission (permissions), Building Dept (new/unsafe buildings), Coroner (fatal accidents/murders), Health Dept (births/deaths/contagious disease), Hotels (important guests), Labor Union HQ (labor news), Shipping Offices (dockings/passengers), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a beat list and know what each source typically yields so coverage is systematic and efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment and Responsibility for Runs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters are assigned 'runs' — specific beats — and are held responsible for all news occurring on their run; failure to cover a beat or being scooped is a serious fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On large papers, specialized watchers may monitor high-volume beats (e.g., police) and relay items to the city editor; reporters must not neglect sources and should visit at appropriate frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Runs (confidential trade sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain runs (garages, delicatessens, florists, caterers) produce news that must be kept 'dark' (confidential) and are fertile for exclusive material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate relationships with tradesmen who learn about private events; use tact to gain exclusive facts. Such sources can reveal incidents otherwise unknown to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Wide Acquaintance and Confidentiality Ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should deliberately cultivate friendships and acquaintances everywhere (stores, cars, clubs) to gather news, but must guard confidences: publish stranger-sourced info, but not confidential tips from friends without permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between publishable information obtained on duty and confidential information from friends; the city editor decides publication when in doubt. Professional integrity and trustworthiness are paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Room Capabilities and Press Efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Press rooms operate complex adaptable presses that can run at full/half/third capacity and perform printing, folding, cutting, pasting, and counting at very high speeds (examples: 50,000 to 125,000 papers per hour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding press capacity and set-up times (e.g., plates fitted half-hour before press time) is important for scheduling and late-news decisions; mechanical capabilities determine how quickly editions can be produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed Devices for Late News (fudge, telegraph composing, advance headlines, held plates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices to publish late news include the 'fudge' (small emergency cylinder printing directly from linotype slugs), composing machines fed by special telegraph wires and operators, and holding pre-set advance headlines/plates until the final moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fudge saves stereotyping time and enables rapid insertion of late copy; papers also prepare alternate heads or hold full plates ready to start presses immediately on receipt of the final flash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation Manager Duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The circulation manager supervises distribution (trains, wagons, newsboys), canvassers for subscriptions, organization of newsboys, and advertising of paper features to build readership; may publish subscription lists or free ads strategically to increase circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success depends on logistical coordination and promotional work to convince readers of the paper's superiority; managers may accept short-term ad revenue loss to grow readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising Manager Duties and Principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The advertising manager sets rates influenced by circulation figures, directs solicitors, advises advertisers on placement/price/space, and has power to accept or reject advertisements (e.g., liquor or questionable ads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuation of ad space depends on page location, neighboring content, and circulation; managers may exchange ads with other papers and publish audited advertising-line statements to attract business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cashier / Counting Room Responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The cashier (counting room) handles payroll, receipts and disbursements, bookkeeping for the publishing company, and payment of bills for paper, ink, machinery, telegraph/telephone, and similar expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cashier typically needs solid bookkeeping and financial skills rather than editorial experience; reporters receive pay envelopes from this office.
